### A day of logging a quantity that barely moves {#sec-t3-why}

Every other thermal experiment on this site asks "what temperature is it?"
This one asks a different question: if you log the *same* sensor, in the
*same* insulated box, for 24 hours, how much does the number wander even
though nothing you would call "the temperature" has changed? What wanders is
the instrument — its own noise, its own slow drift — and the room around the
box, which does change, on a cycle you already know the period of.

The box is insulated for the same reason S1 shorted an input to ground: to
remove the source and look at what the measurement chain contributes on its
own. Insulation does not remove the room's diurnal cycle, it *attenuates* it,
which is why the diurnal cycle is still the largest feature in the record —
see @sec-t3-drift — and is not a failure of the rig.

### Separating drift from the diurnal cycle {#sec-t3-drift}

The record is fit, by ordinary least squares, to a model with four
parameters: a mean level, a linear drift, and a sinusoid at exactly the
period of a day,

$$
x(t) = x_0 + \dot{x}\,t + A_d\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{P_d} + \phi_d\right) + \varepsilon(t)
$$ {#eq-t3-fit}

with $P_d = 24\ \mathrm{h}$ fixed (not fitted — it is a property of the
Earth, not of the instrument), $\dot{x}$ the **drift**, reported in mK/h, and
$\varepsilon(t)$ everything the deterministic model does not explain. Fitting
$A_d$ and $\phi_d$ together with $\dot x$ in one least-squares problem, rather
than fitting a line first and eyeballing the rest, is what keeps a slow part
of the diurnal cycle from being absorbed into the drift estimate — the two
are only cleanly separable because $P_d$ is known exactly and $\dot x$ is (for
an insulated box, over one day) very small by comparison.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The four-parameter fit is linear in its parameters once $P_d$ is fixed — the
design matrix has columns $[1,\ t,\ \cos(2\pi t/P_d),\ \sin(2\pi t/P_d)]$ —
so it is solved in one step by ordinary least squares, exactly as S1's
three-parameter calibration fit is. Nothing here is iterative, unlike S2's
sine fit, because the frequency is known rather than estimated.
:::

What is left over, $\varepsilon(t)$, is what @sec-t3-allan characterizes. Fit
and subtract the model *before* computing an Allan deviation on it: a
diurnal cycle left in the record would show up as extra curvature at long
averaging times and could be mistaken for the instrument's own random walk,
which is a different mechanism with a different consequence (@sec-t3-slope).

### The overlapping Allan deviation {#sec-t3-allan}

The question this experiment exists to answer is: *if I average this signal
for longer, does my answer get better, and for how long does that keep being
true?* A plain standard deviation of the whole record answers a different
question — how spread out the values are — and says nothing about *when* in
time that spread accumulates. The Allan deviation [@allan1966] does: it is a
function of the averaging time $\tau$, built from the second difference of
the record at that averaging time, and its shape identifies the noise
process responsible at each $\tau$.

Take the residual $\varepsilon(t)$ as a stream of samples at spacing
$\tau_0$ and form its **overlapping Allan variance** at averaging time
$\tau = m\tau_0$ ($m = 1, 2, 3, \dots$):

$$
\sigma_y^2(\tau) = \frac{1}{2(N-2m)\,\tau^2}
  \sum_{i=1}^{N-2m}\left(\bar{x}_{i+2m} - 2\bar{x}_{i+m} + \bar{x}_i\right)^2
$$ {#eq-t3-allan}

with $\bar{x}_i$ the **integrated** (phase-like) samples,
$\bar{x}_i = \tau_0\sum_{k=1}^{i}\varepsilon_k$ — the running sum of the
residual record, not the residual itself. This is the standard, numerically
stable way to evaluate @eq-t3-allan from a record of *rate-like* samples
(here, a temperature reading is the analogue of a fractional frequency
$y$): integrate once to get a phase-like $\bar x$, then take the doubled,
overlapping second difference. "Overlapping" means every valid starting index
$i$ is used, not just every $m$-th one, which uses the record far more
efficiently than the non-overlapping estimator and is why 24 h of data at a
few-second sample interval is enough to see a clean curve.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Two things about @eq-t3-allan worth being deliberate about. First, computing
it directly at every $i$ for every $m$ is $O(N \times M)$, which is entirely
tractable here — the sums for a fixed $m$ are cheap vector operations, and
neither language needs a library implementation. Second, the choice of which
$m$ values to evaluate is free; a logarithmically spaced set from $m=1$ up to
around $N/4$ gives an even spread of points on the log-log plot without
computing $\sigma_y(\tau)$ at every possible $\tau$, most of which would be
redundant this close together.
:::

### Reading the slope {#sec-t3-slope}

On a log-log plot of $\sigma_y(\tau)$ against $\tau$, the slope identifies
the noise process, because each one has its own, different power-law
dependence on averaging time:

| Slope | Noise process | What is happening |
|:--:|---|---|
| $\tau^{-1/2}$ | White (uncorrelated) noise | Independent samples average down exactly as $s/\sqrt{n}$ would predict |
| $\tau^{0}$ | Flicker noise | Averaging buys nothing more; the noise has memory on every timescale |
| $\tau^{+1/2}$ | Random walk | The instrument's own slow wander accumulates *faster* the longer you average |

: Allan-deviation slopes and their causes {#tbl-t3-slopes}

A record with both a white and a random-walk component — which is the
plausible minimum for a real instrument, and what @sec-t3-why's synthetic
data is built from — produces a curve that falls, flattens, and rises again:
falling while averaging beats down the white noise, rising once the random
walk starts to dominate. The **minimum of that curve is the optimum
averaging time** $\tau_\mathrm{opt}$. Past it, more averaging makes the
answer *worse* — this is the single most counter-intuitive, and most useful,
result in the experiment, because it contradicts the assumption every
earlier experiment on this site has quietly relied on: that longer is
always better.

### Connecting to S1 {#sec-t3-s1}

[S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd) showed the Type A term of a static
measurement falling as $1/\sqrt{n}$ and concluded that beyond a few hundred
samples, more averaging bought essentially nothing — because by then the
Type A term had dropped below the calibration and quantization terms. T3
shows *why* $1/\sqrt{n}$ is only ever a short-averaging-time approximation in
the first place: it is the white-noise slope of @tbl-t3-slopes, valid only
up to $\tau_\mathrm{opt}$, and it shows where, in absolute averaging time,
that approximation stops being merely dominated by other terms (S1's
situation) and starts being **wrong on its own terms** (T3's).

### Why the Type A term is not $s/\sqrt{n}$ {#sec-t3-typea}

The ordinary formula $s/\sqrt{n}$ for the standard uncertainty of a mean
assumes the $n$ samples averaged are independent. A record with a
random-walk component is, by construction, *not* independent from one sample
to the next — each value is the last one plus a small step — so
$s/\sqrt{n}$, evaluated over the whole 24 h record, understates how much the
mean can still move, sometimes by a large factor, because it is answering a
question ("how spread out are individual samples?") that was never the
question the budget needs answered ("how well is the mean of this particular
average known?").

The Allan deviation answers the right question directly: $\sigma_y(\tau)$ *is*
the standard uncertainty of an average taken over a window of length $\tau$,
correctly accounting for the correlation between samples inside that window.
Evaluating it at $\tau_\mathrm{opt}$ therefore gives the best Type A term this
record can support — and using any $\tau$ larger than $\tau_\mathrm{opt}$ in
[the budget](handbook.qmd#sec-t3-budget) would be using a number the
experiment has already shown to be pessimistic on purpose.
